summary: This informational document discusses how centralization relates to Internet standards work. It argues that standards bodies have limited power to prevent many forms of centralization, but they can still contribute to making the Internet more decentralized.

plainLanguage.summary: If only a few big companies control the internet, that can be unfair. This asks what rule-makers can do to help many people share control.

questions: what is centralization in internet standards
what can standards bodies do about centralization
subtitle: What role can standards play in resisting the concentration of Internet control?

tldr.problem: The Internet was designed without a central control point, but many Internet services today are dominated by a few large companies. Standards bodies like the IETF have limited power to prevent this centralization through protocol design alone, yet they remain central to how the Internet evolves.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9518 examines why centralization happens, why decentralization is difficult, and what concrete steps standards can take: bolstering their own legitimacy with policymakers, focusing discussions on specific technical facts, targeting proprietary functions with standardized alternatives, making it easy for users to switch between implementations, controlling what power is delegated to intermediaries, and reusing successful patterns.
tldr.outcome: Standards bodies can better serve decentralization by acknowledging that technical standards alone are insufficient and by working strategically on the aspects of Internet design where they can have real impact, often in concert with regulation and market forces.

today: RFC 9518 was published in December 2023 as an informational document expressing the author's views rather than IETF consensus. It has been widely discussed in the Internet standards community and serves as a reference for conversations about protocol design and centralization in standards bodies, government regulators considering Internet policy, and engineers designing new protocols.

sections.title: Why decentralization matters and why it is slipping away
sections.content:
The Internet was designed to have no single point of control. Early on, services like email and USENET had multiple competing providers that could interoperate with each other. Today, many Internet services—social networks, marketplaces, messaging platforms—are operated by single companies with no interoperable alternatives. People sometimes mistake these services for "the Internet" itself. This concentration of control creates risks: a company can exploit its position, experiment on users without oversight, exclude competitors, or be coerced by governments in ways that smaller providers cannot.

The RFC asks what role Internet standards bodies can play in this landscape. The question is vital because standards bodies like the IETF have shaped the Internet's evolution, yet the most powerful services today operate on standards (like HTTP) that do not prevent centralization. The answer is not that standards bodies are powerless, but that their power is real yet limited and works best when combined with other forces.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if only one company ran the telephone network. They could listen in, charge unfair prices, or shut you off if they dislike you. The Internet was meant to prevent this by having many equal networks, but today a few companies control what billions of people see and say online.

sections.title: Why centralization can be harmful
sections.content:
Centralization can cause real harms. When one entity controls how people communicate, it gains the panopticon effect—the ability to watch what everyone does—and the chokepoint effect—the ability to block or alter communication. This power imbalance can be exploited for coercion, surveillance, or discrimination. Centralized services can limit innovation by requiring newcomers to get permission from the gatekeeper. Competition suffers when users cannot easily switch to alternatives, making the dominant service an "essential facility" that can exploit its position. Availability risks emerge because a single company's failure affects everyone. A monoculture means a single codebase's bug can break services for millions. Finally, centralized providers reinforce their dominance by using their scale to gather data and improve their products while blocking the same access to competitors.

However, the RFC emphasizes that these harms are complex. For example, centralization can sometimes improve availability because a large provider has more resources, yet it can also create larger-scale failures. The analysis requires nuance in each case.
sections.plainLanguage: A monopoly can decide what you see, charge unfair prices, and there is nowhere else to go. If everyone uses the same code and it breaks, millions of people are stuck at once.

sections.title: When centralization is necessary and beneficial
sections.content:
Some Internet functions require or benefit from centralization for technical or economic reasons. The DNS root is by nature a single global "source of truth"—it must have one authority to translate domain names into addresses in a consistent way across the world. IP address allocation must be coordinated globally to ensure unique addresses; if captured by one actor, the whole Internet could be at risk. Certificate Authorities serve as trust anchors for secure web connections, creating centralization that is necessary for security. Rendezvous functions (like chat servers that help two users find each other) often require a third party, which is inherently centralized.

Beyond necessity, centralization can bring benefits: economies of scale can lower costs and improve quality, specialized organizations can manage complex and risky functions better, governance structures can impose community standards, and focused attention can improve reliability. When centralization is broadly considered necessary or beneficial and has oversight mechanisms, it may be appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: One global phone book makes sense—you need one place to look up numbers consistently. One authority deciding which websites are trustworthy can protect people from fraud.

sections.title: Why decentralization is hard and incomplete
sections.content:
Decentralized technical design is necessary but not sufficient to create decentralized outcomes. Federation (the ability to run your own server and connect with others) is a good design pattern, but non-technical forces can concentrate power anyway. Email, which is federated, has become dominated by a few large providers because running an email server requires expertise, fighting spam is resource-intensive, and large providers have power imbalances over small ones. XMPP chat is federated in theory, but major providers chose not to interoperate with others, locking in their users.

Distributed consensus technologies like blockchains can decentralize operation, but other aspects remain centralized: governance of the protocol, creation of reference implementations, and design decisions still require coordination. Some blockchain systems show high concentration in mining power or wealth despite their decentralized machinery.

Attempts to decentralize often shift centralization elsewhere—from operation to governance, from design to deployment, or from one layer to another. Different people disagree on what "sufficiently decentralized" means. Governance structures like ICANN's multi-stakeholder oversight of the DNS can be seen as legitimate oversight or as an unelected authority depending on perspective.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if you can set up your own email server, you might not want to because it is complicated and hard to get your emails delivered to big email companies that don't like you.

sections.title: Eight concrete steps for standards bodies
sections.content: Rather than futilely trying to prevent all centralization, standards bodies should take specific actions where they have real leverage. Bolster legitimacy so policymakers trust their technical advice; this requires inclusive participation and transparent processes. Focus discussions on specific, verifiable technical facts rather than sweeping claims about centralization. Target proprietary functions with new standards—if only one company offers chat, standardize chat to enable competition. Enable switching by making standards functionally complete and precise enough that users can substitute one implementation for another without major costs. Control delegation of power by designing systems where third-party intermediaries (if needed) are explicit and limited to what they must do. Enforce boundaries using encryption so lower-layer network operators cannot discriminate against applications. Consider extensibility carefully—do not make a protocol so flexible that vendors can require proprietary extensions to make it useful. Reuse what works by incorporating proven governance patterns (like DNS) rather than reinventing decentralization each time.
sections.plainLanguage: Standards makers can help by making rules that let people switch to different companies, by talking to governments about what rules actually work, and by not letting one company force everyone to use their special add-ons.

items.title: Power Imbalance
items.text: The gatekeeper gains power to observe, block, or alter communication for coercive ends.

items.title: Limited Innovation
items.text: New applications need permission from the central authority, not just from other developers.

items.title: Reduced Competition
items.text: Users cannot easily switch when a service becomes an "essential facility."

items.title: Monoculture Risk
items.text: A single codebase's bug or vulnerability can break the service for millions at once.
